# Session 5 · Data: collect it well, describe it honestly

## Week 5 · Saturday

- Recap quiz on Sessions 3-4 (10 min)
- 5.1 Good data by design: variables, CRF, data dictionary, checks, data management
- 5.2 Meet the course dataset FLUID-ICU (live R cleaning demo)
- 5.3 Describing and showing data: summaries, figures, tables
- 5.4 Describe the course dataset: Table 1 and figures
- Proposal builder 5: variables, mini-CRF, data dictionary, data management

::: {.notes}
Session 5 (19:30-22:30, break 20:40-20:55). Today the data, next Saturday the analysis.

New: the simulated course dataset FLUID-ICU (620 adults with sepsis) and five questions, Q1 to Q5. At the end of Session 6 each participant chooses one and writes its Results section.

No formulas: picture, worked example, check. Never skip the checks.
:::

## Recap quiz: Sessions 3-4 in three questions

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 10 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Q1. Patients who smoke are followed for 10 years to see who develops a stroke. Which design?
- Q2. In a cohort, sicker septic patients receive more fluid and die more often. What is this called?
- Q3. Mortality is 30% with usual care and 20% with a new strategy. What are the risk ratio (RR) and the number needed to treat (NNT)?
- Answer each question in the poll (1 minute each), then we discuss
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone back on track with designs, confounding and the 2x2 measures
:::

::: {.notes}
Recap (19:30-19:40). One poll per question, 1 minute each. Show the results, then the next slide, and ask one volunteer to explain.
:::

## Recap quiz: answers

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Q1. Prospective cohort]{.neu-card-title}

- Starts from the exposure (smoking)
- Follows people forward to stroke
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Q2. Confounding by indication]{.neu-card-title}

- Severity drives both fluid and death
- Why Paper 2 used propensity matching
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Q3. RR 0.67, NNT 10]{.neu-card-title}

- RR = 20/30 = 0.67
- RD = 10%, so NNT = 1/0.10 = 10
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Case-control starts from the outcome. A cohort starts from the exposure.
:::

::: {.notes}
If a third got Q3 wrong, draw the 2x2 table on screen.

Timing: within the 10 minutes of the recap.
:::

## 5.1 Good data by design

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
Bad data cannot be rescued by good statistics.
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
5.1 Good data by design  \|  35 minutes
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Section 5.1 (19:40-20:15).

Message: most problems lie in the data, not the analysis. A statistician cannot fix a blank box later.

Ask: who has been asked to 'help with the data' and found half the forms incomplete?
:::

**KEY MESSAGE** No method can fix wrong data. Get the data right first.
:::

::: {.notes}
Garbage in, garbage out, with one number from the course dataset.

Top row: the raw file as the four ICUs sent it. ICU C wrote lactate in mg/dL, and 999 and -99 were typed for 'not done'. The mean comes out at 28.4 mmol/L, which no patient has.

Bottom row: the same mean on the clean file gives 2.9 mmol/L.

Ask: would a more advanced model have caught this? Expected: no, it would give a wrong answer with more decimals.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## What type of variable is it?

::: {.neu-intro}
Numbers are measured (first two cards). Categories are groups (last three). Time-to-event combines how long and whether it happened.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Continuous]{.neu-card-title}

- Any value on a scale
- Fluid balance (ml/kg), lactate, age
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Count]{.neu-card-title}

- A whole number
- Number of organ failures
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Binary]{.neu-card-title}

- Two options
- Died by day 28: yes or no
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Nominal]{.neu-card-title}

- Groups with no order
- Source of sepsis: lung, urine, abdomen
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Ordinal]{.neu-card-title}

- Groups in an order
- Acute kidney injury (AKI) stage 1, 2 or 3
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The variable type decides the CRF box, the summary and the test.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every variable is a number (continuous, count) or a category (binary, nominal, ordinal). Time-to-event: just mention it, it returns in Session 6.

Misconception: sex coded 1/2 is still a category.

Tip: collect numbers as numbers. You can group age later, never ungroup it.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## Check your understanding: what type of variable?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Heart rate (beats per minute)
- Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS, 3-15)
- Blood group (A, B, AB, O)
- Ventilated on day 1 (yes / no)
- Time from ICU admission to extubation
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Continuous
- Count
- Binary
- Nominal
- Ordinal
- Time-to-event
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One poll vote per variable: everyone can name the variable types
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (3 minutes). One poll per variable, with the six options on the right. Show the results, then the answers on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: what type of variable?

| Variable | Type | Why |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Heart rate | Continuous | A measured number |
| GCS (3-15) | Ordinal | Ordered levels, often analysed as a number |
| Blood group | Nominal | Categories with no order |
| Ventilated on day 1 | Binary | Two options: yes or no |
| Time to extubation | Time-to-event | Some patients are never extubated |

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The variable type decides the CRF box, the summary and the test.
:::

::: {.notes}
If a third got it wrong, go back one slide.

Timing: within the 3 minutes of the check.
:::

::: {.notes}
A good CRF item: two people filling it for the same patient write the same answer.

Ask the class what is wrong with each left-hand item, then point to the red note under it: no unit or time window, age without a date, incomplete options, two opinions in one question.

Ask: what is wrong with a blank box? Expected: 'not done', 'forgot' and 'zero' look the same.
:::

## Worked example: from a question to one CRF item

::: {.neu-intro}
The variable 'cumulative fluid balance' in five decisions:
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[What?]{.neu-step-label}

- Fluid in minus fluid out
- All routes, including drug diluents
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[When?]{.neu-step-label}

- From ICU admission to the end of day 3
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Unit?]{.neu-step-label}

- ml per kg of admission weight
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Format?]{.neu-step-label}

- A number with a +/- sign
- One box per digit
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[Missing?]{.neu-step-label}

- A 'not recorded' box
- A reason for the gap
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Answer what, when, unit, format and missing before the first patient.
:::

::: {.notes}
Worked example (3 minutes): the FLUID-ICU exposure in five decisions.

What: all fluid in minus all fluid out. When: ICU admission to end of day 3. Unit: ml/kg of admission weight. Format: a signed number. Missing: a 'not recorded' box.

Ask: which item must the CRF now also contain? Expected: weight at admission.
:::

## Five rules for a good CRF

::: {.neu-intro}
Write the form before the first patient, then test it on five patients.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Only what you need]{.neu-card-title}

- Every item links to an objective
- Short forms get completed
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[One question, one answer]{.neu-card-title}

- No double questions
- Objective, not opinion
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Units and timing]{.neu-card-title}

- ml/kg, mmol/L
- 'at ICU admission', 'day 5'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Closed answers]{.neu-card-title}

- Tick boxes
- Include 'other' and 'unknown'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Pilot it]{.neu-card-title}

- Two people, same patient
- Do they agree?
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** If two colleagues can fill an item differently, rewrite it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the five card titles with one example each.

Common mistake: changing the form after data collection has started gives two different datasets.

Ask: which rule is most often broken in your unit? Expected: too long, no units, free text.
:::

## The data dictionary: one row per variable

| Variable name | Label (meaning) | Type | Unit / codes | Allowed values |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| fb\_d5 | Cumulative fluid balance, day 5 | Continuous | ml/kg | -100 to 300 |
| age | Age at ICU admission | Continuous | years | 18 to 110 |
| sex | Sex | Binary | 1 = male, 2 = female | 1, 2 |
| src | Main source of infection | Nominal | 1 lung, 2 urine, 3 abdomen, 4 other, 9 unknown | 1 to 4, 9 |
| died28 | Died by day 28 | Binary | 0 = alive, 1 = died | 0, 1 |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Example rows for the fluids-in-septic-shock study. The data dictionary is the instruction manual for your dataset.
:::

::: {.notes}
The data dictionary: one row per variable, so anyone can understand the data without phoning you.

Read the age row aloud. Its allowed values, 18 to 110, become the range check on the next slide. Note the 'unknown' code 9 in the src row.

Participants write 3 to 5 rows like these in Proposal builder 5.
:::

## Data validation: let the rules catch the errors

::: {.neu-intro}
Four simple checks catch most data-entry errors.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Range check]{.neu-card-title}

- Age = 230
- Allowed: 18 to 110
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Consistency check]{.neu-card-title}

- Discharge 02/03, admission 05/03
- Discharge must come after admission
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Logic check]{.neu-card-title}

- Sex = male, pregnant = yes
- An impossible combination
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Completeness check]{.neu-card-title}

- Day-28 status left blank
- A required field: chase it now
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Check data while the patient is still in the unit, not a year later.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four checks catch most entry errors: range, consistency, logic, completeness. The range comes from the data dictionary.

Find errors while the chart is still on the ward.

Ask: what impossible values have you seen? Expected: 700 kg, future dates.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Data management in practice: from bedside to database

::: {.neu-intro}
Two safe routes from the patient to one secure database.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Paper CRF]{.neu-card-title}

- Double data entry: two people type each form
- A computer compares the two copies
- Mismatches are fixed from the paper form
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Electronic data capture (EDC)]{.neu-card-title}

- Form on a tablet or computer
- For example REDCap or KoBoToolbox
- Range, logic and required-field checks at entry
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Secure database]{.neu-card-title}

- Coded study IDs, no names
- Audit trail: who changed what, when and why
- Example: lactate 21 corrected to 2.1, 'typo'
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Check at entry, enter twice if on paper, and log every change.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two safe routes: paper with double data entry, or electronic data capture (REDCap, KoBoToolbox) with checks at entry.

The database holds study codes, never names, and keeps an audit trail.

Ask: who has seen an Excel file with names and results emailed around?

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Missing data are rarely random: the sickest patients go missing first.
:::

::: {.notes}
Missing data, part 1. Walk the picture: 30% truly died, but 15 deaths have an empty box, so we see 18%.

Missing is linked to the outcome: the sickest go missing first. Who is missing matters more than how many.

Mechanisms and imputation come in 6.4.
:::

## Missing data: how to prevent it

::: {.neu-intro}
Prevention is the only reliable cure.
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Fewer items]{.neu-step-label}

- Collect only what you need
- Short forms get finished
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Clear form]{.neu-step-label}

- Required fields marked
- 'Not done' and 'unknown' options
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Train]{.neu-step-label}

- Train every data collector
- Same rules, same definitions
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Check weekly]{.neu-step-label}

- A completeness report
- Who and what is missing?
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[Chase early]{.neu-step-label}

- Fix while the chart is on the ward
- Plan follow-up for transfers
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Plan who completes, checks and chases each form before you start.
:::

::: {.notes}
Missing data, part 2: five habits prevent most of it.

The day-28 outcome is the most often missing variable in ICU studies: plan who checks it for transfers.

These steps go into the data-quality plan of Proposal Part 3.
:::

::: {.neu-big}
One realistic dataset, five research questions.

5.2 Meet the course dataset FLUID-ICU  \|  25 minutes

::::

::: {.notes}
Section 5.2 (20:15-20:40).

FLUID-ICU is simulated: no real patient, hospital or country, but it behaves like real ICU data.

Nobody runs R. The instructor does it on screen.

Ask: what can a cohort claim that a trial cannot? Expected: association, not causation.
:::

## FLUID-ICU at a glance (simulated cohort)

::: {.neu-intro}
A multicentre prospective cohort in 4 intensive care units (ICUs), January 2023 to December 2024.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Who]{.neu-card-title}

- 620 adults with sepsis
- ICU A 191, ICU B 164, ICU C 147, ICU D 118
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Exposure]{.neu-card-title}

- Cumulative fluid balance by day 3 (ml/kg)
- Positive in 373/618 (60.4%)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Primary outcome]{.neu-card-title}

- Death by day 28: 179/620 (28.9%)
- Time to death also recorded
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Also recorded]{.neu-card-title}

- Severity scores (SOFA, APACHE II)
- Lactate
- Acute kidney injury (AKI)
- Ventilator-free days, ICU stay
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Question: is a positive fluid balance by day 3 associated with 28-day death?
:::

::: {.notes}
Know the study before any analysis.

620 adults with sepsis, 4 ICUs, 2023-2024. Exposure: cumulative fluid balance by day 3, positive in 373 of 618 (60.4%). Primary outcome: death by day 28, 179 of 620 (28.9%).

Ask: who do you expect to have a positive balance? Expected: the sickest. Keep it for Table 1.
:::

## From 623 rows to 527 complete cases

::: {.neu-intro}
FLUID-ICU (simulated): who is included at each step, and why not.
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Raw file]{.neu-step-label}

- 623 rows
- Minus 3 duplicate records
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Enrolled]{.neu-step-label}

- 620 patients
- Minus 2 without a day-3 fluid balance
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Exposure analysis]{.neu-step-label}

- 618 patients (Table 1, comparisons)
- Minus 91 without lactate (or age)
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Complete cases]{.neu-step-label}

- 527 patients
- Used for the adjusted model
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Every paper reports this flow: who was included at each step, and why not.
:::

::: {.notes}
The flow of patients: 623 rows, 3 duplicates removed, 620 enrolled. 2 without a day-3 balance: 618 analysed. 91 without lactate or age: 527 in the adjusted model.

Ask: where does this flow go in a paper? Expected: the first paragraph of the Results. Every Results section starts here.
:::

## Raw vs clean: what the four ICUs actually sent

| Problem | Raw file (as sent) | Clean file (01\_clean.R) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Sex | 8 spellings: M, m, male, F, f ... | Male / Female |
| Yes / No | Yes, Y, yes, 1  \|  No, N, no, 0 | Yes / No |
| Admission date | 2023-03-14 \| 14/03/2023 \| 14-Mar-2023 | 2023-03-14 |
| Lactate, ICU C | 23.4  (mg/dL) | 2.6  (mmol/L) |
| Missing codes | 999  \|  -99 | missing (NA) |
| Impossible | age 210 \| weight 7 kg \| output -2990 ml | missing + query to site |
| Duplicates | 623 rows (3 IDs twice) | 620 patients |

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Real data arrive messy: clean them with a script, never by hand.
:::

::: {.notes}
Go row by row. For each problem, ask what it would do to the analysis before you point to the clean column.

Each problem breaks the analysis silently: 999 inflates a mean, 'Y' and 'Yes' become two groups, mg/dL makes ICU C look like a disaster.

Impossible values are set to missing with a query to the site. We never guess.
:::

## Live demo: cleaning FLUID-ICU in R

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#B5651D"}
LIVE DEMO · 8 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#B5651D"}
- Open FLUID-ICU.Rproj and the script 01\_clean.R
- Read the raw file as text and look at it
- Run one block per problem: names, duplicates, sites, dates, codes
- Find the lactate unit problem with a summary by ICU
- Last block: the cleaned file is identical to the reference file
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#B5651D"}
Watch for

- One problem, one block
- The raw file is never changed
- Every step goes in the log
- Re-run = same result
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#B5651D"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone has seen raw data become clean, reproducibly
:::

::: {.notes}
Live demo, 8 minutes. Script and fallback screenshots: s5\_demo.md, Part A.

Run one block at a time and say what it fixes. Ask the class to predict first.

Three points: the raw file is never edited, one problem one block, a script gives the same result every time.

Stop at 8 minutes.
:::

## The cleaning log: the audit trail of the data

::: {.neu-intro}
cleaning\_log.md: one row for every change made to the raw data.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[The rule]{.neu-card-title}

- Never edit the raw file
- Every change is made by the script and logged
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Each row says]{.neu-card-title}

- The problem found
- How many records
- What we did and why
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Queries]{.neu-card-title}

- Impossible value set to missing
- Query sent to the site
- The patient stays in
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[What is left]{.neu-card-title}

- Real missing values
- Lactate: 93/620 (15.0%)
- Others: 1% or less
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Anyone who checks the data must be able to trace every number back to the raw data.
:::

::: {.notes}
The cleaning log (cleaning\_log.md): one row per change, with the reason.

Impossible values are set to missing and queried. The patient stays in.

What is left is real missing data: lactate 93 of 620 (15.0%).

Ask: why not delete the patient aged 210? Expected: the rest of the record is valid.
:::

## Five questions, one dataset

::: {.neu-intro}
In class we work through all five together. At the end of Session 6 you choose one.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Q1 Mortality]{.neu-card-title}

- Positive balance and 28-day death
- Outcome: binary, and time to death
- Analysis: logistic regression, Kaplan-Meier and Cox
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Q2 Kidneys]{.neu-card-title}

- Fluid balance and acute kidney injury (AKI)
- Outcome: binary, AKI yes or no
- Analysis: logistic regression
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Q3 Ventilation]{.neu-card-title}

- Fluid balance and ventilator-free days
- Outcome: days from 0 to 28, skewed
- Analysis: Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) and linear regression
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Q4 Lactate]{.neu-card-title}

- Lactate and 28-day death
- Outcome: binary. Lactate missing in 15%
- Analysis: logistic regression, complete case and multiple imputation
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Q5 ICU stay]{.neu-card-title}

- Fluid balance and ICU stay in survivors
- Outcome: days, skewed
- Analysis: Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) and regression on the log scale
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** We give you the results. You write the Results section for the question you choose.
:::

::: {.notes}
One dataset, five questions, all from the FLUID-ICU SAP. Each card gives the question, the type of outcome and the analysis.

AKI in Q2 is yes or no (KDIGO stage 1 or more), so binary logistic regression. The stage itself (0 to 3) is ordinal, which would call for ordinal logistic regression, not multinomial.

Q1 (the primary question) is done in full in Sessions 5 and 6. Q2 to Q5 more briefly.

Each question has a results pack (Results\_Pack\_Q1 to Q5, PDF, sent by email).

At the end of Session 6 each participant chooses one question and writes its Results section from the pack.
:::

## 5.3 Describing and showing data

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
Before comparing groups, describe them.
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
5.3 Describing and showing data  \|  35 minutes
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Section 5.3 (20:55-21:30).

Message: every numerical variable needs a centre and a spread. The shape of the data decides which pair: mean (SD) or median (IQR).
:::

## Worked example: mean and median by hand

::: {.neu-intro}
ICU stay of 7 patients (days): 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 6, 24
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Line up]{.neu-step-label}

- Sort from the shortest to the longest stay
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Median]{.neu-step-label}

- The 4th of 7 patients: 3 days
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Mean]{.neu-step-label}

- 42 days / 7 patients = 6 days
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Compare]{.neu-step-label}

- One 24-day stay doubles the mean
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** One very long stay moves the mean a lot and the median not at all.
:::

::: {.notes}
Worked example (3 minutes). Type the seven stays on screen.

Median: the 4th patient, 3 days. Mean: 42 / 7 = 6 days. One long stay doubles the mean.

Ask: if that patient stayed 60 days? Expected: median still 3, mean about 11.

The only hand calculation today.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** For skewed data like length of stay, the median describes the typical patient.
:::

::: {.notes}
Most patients stay 1 to 5 days, a few for weeks: the mean (3.9) is pulled right of the median (2.8).

Rule of thumb: mean and median far apart means skewed: report the median.

Ask: other skewed variables in your work? Expected: costs, CRP, days on ventilator.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Report mean (SD) or median (IQR): never mix the pairs.
:::

::: {.notes}
Symmetric data: mean (SD). Skewed data: median (IQR), the middle half of patients.

Read 'median 2.8 (IQR 1.5 to 4.7)' aloud in plain words.

Common mistakes: mean with IQR, median with SD, and confusing SD (spread of patients) with a CI (precision, 6.1).
:::

## Why these two shapes? They cover most clinical data

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Most clinical data cluster around a typical value or have a long tail. Check which.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two shapes cover most clinical data: symmetric (physiology, body size) and right-skewed (times, counts, costs, lab values that cannot go below zero).

The shape also decides the test in 6.1.

Ask: days on vasopressors, symmetric or skewed? Expected: skewed.
:::

## Check your understanding: which summary?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- ICU length of stay in 200 patients: mean (SD) or median (IQR)?
- Age of 200 adult ICU patients, bell-shaped: mean (SD) or median (IQR)?
- Ventilated on admission (yes/no): which summary?
- Acute kidney injury (AKI) stage 1 to 3: which summary and which graph?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Mean (SD)
- Median (IQR)
- n (%)
- Bar chart or histogram
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One poll vote per item: the right summary for each variable type
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (3 minutes), one poll per item. Show the results, then the answers on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: which summary?

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Median (IQR)]{.neu-card-title}

- ICU stay is skewed
- A few patients stay very long
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Mean (SD)]{.neu-card-title}

- Age is bell-shaped
- So the mean fits
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[n (%)]{.neu-card-title}

- Yes or no
- Count and percent
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[n (%) per stage]{.neu-card-title}

- Ordered categories: bar chart
- Never a 'mean stage'
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Skewed: median (IQR). Bell-shaped: mean (SD). Categories: n (%).
:::

::: {.notes}
If many missed item 1, return to the histogram.

Timing: within the 3 minutes of the check.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Choose the graph from the variable type, not from the software menu.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four graphs cover most needs: bar chart (one category), histogram (one number), boxplots (a number by group), scatter plot (two numbers).

Ask: which graph compares ICU stay between two fluid groups? Expected: side-by-side boxplots.
:::


::: {.notes}
The dynamite plot hides the shape and the outlier. The dots show one patient at 160 ml/kg dragging the mean and a large overlap.

Always say whether error bars are SD, SE or 95% CI.

Ask: what would you conclude from the left picture alone?

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## What a 'Table 1' shows

| Characteristic | Restrictive (n = 24) | Usual care (n = 24) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Age, years, mean (SD) | 64 (11) | 66 (12) |
| Male, n (%) | 15 (63) | 16 (67) |
| SOFA score, median (IQR) | 9 (7-11) | 9 (6-12) |
| Lactate, mmol/L, median (IQR) | 3.1 (2.2-4.8) | 2.9 (2.0-5.1) |
| Source: lung, n (%) | 11 (46) | 10 (42) |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Illustrative numbers. Symmetric: mean (SD). Skewed: median (IQR). Categories: n (%). SD = standard deviation. IQR = interquartile range. SOFA = Sequential Organ Failure Assessment. Ask: who were the patients, and were the groups alike at the start?
:::

::: {.notes}
Table 1 describes the patients at baseline, by group. The summary is in the row label.

Two questions: do these patients look like mine, and were the groups alike at the start?

In a trial, differences are chance (no p-values). In a cohort, large differences warn of confounding.

Numbers are illustrative.
:::

::: {.notes}
A table must stand alone. Compare row by row: group names and n in the header, unit and summary in each row label, sensible decimals, footnotes for abbreviations.

Ask: find four problems in the left table in 30 seconds.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## FLUID-ICU Table 1: were the groups alike at the start?

| Characteristic | Overall
n = 618 | Negative balance
n = 245 | Positive balance
n = 373 |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Age, years, mean (SD) | 62.6 (15.2) | 64.6 (15.0) | 61.4 (15.2) |
| Male sex, n (%) | 375 (61%) | 143 (58%) | 232 (62%) |
| Heart failure, n (%) | 97 (16%) | 54 (22%) | 43 (12%) |
| **SOFA score, median (IQR)** | **[7 (5, 9)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[6 (4, 8)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[8 (6, 10)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** |
| **Lactate, mmol/L, median (IQR)** | **[2.6 (1.7, 3.7)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[2.2 (1.4, 3.0)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[2.9 (1.9, 4.0)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** |
| **Vasopressor, n (%)** | **[266 (43%)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[61 (25%)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[205 (55%)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** |
| **Mechanical ventilation, n (%)** | **[313 (51%)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[97 (40%)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** | **[216 (58%)]{style="color:#0B376C"}** |

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The positive-balance group was sicker at baseline: a warning for Session 6.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read with the two questions from 5.3.

Age similar. Severity not: SOFA 6 vs 8, vasopressor 24.9% vs 55.0%, ventilation 39.6% vs 57.9%. Heart failure goes the other way (22.0% vs 11.5%).

Sicker patients got more fluid: confounding by indication.

Ask: crude OR larger or smaller than adjusted? Expected: larger.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A continuous exposure, cut at 0 ml/kg into negative and positive balance.
:::

::: {.notes}
Made by 02\_describe.R, block 4. Look at the exposure before using it: the black line is the median, 8.8 ml/kg, and the grey band the IQR, -10.3 to 26.2. Positive in 373 of 618.

Q1 cuts it at 0 ml/kg. Q2 and Q3 keep it continuous (per 10 ml/kg). The SAP fixed this in advance.
:::

Made by 02\_describe.R, block 5. Dots plus box for FLUID-ICU: median SOFA 6 vs 8, every patient visible.

Ask: why not a bar of the mean SOFA? Expected: it would hide the spread and the overlap.

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Mean 7.5 vs median 6.2 days: report the median and IQR.
:::

::: {.notes}
Made by 02\_describe.R, block 7. ICU stay in the 439 survivors is right-skewed: mean 7.5, median 6.2 days.

Q5 reports medians (IQR), uses Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) and a log scale in the model.

Every Table 1 has at least one skewed variable.
:::

## Exercise: read the FLUID-ICU Table 1

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#0D7377"}
WHOLE-CLASS TASK · 10 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#0D7377"}
- Table 1 of FLUID-ICU, in the Q1 results pack (exercise sheet, Exercise 6). The Q4 and Q5 packs have a different Table 1
- Which summaries does it use, were the groups alike at the start, and how would you describe the patients?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
Check

- n per column?
- Units in labels?
- Median for skewed?
- Missing reported?
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0D7377"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (5 min): answer questions 1 to 5, ending with two Results sentences
:::

::: {.notes}
Whole class, 10 minutes (21:45-21:55). Exercise 6. Answers: s5\_solutions.md.

5 minutes: everyone works alone. Then 4 minutes: call on two or three people for the summaries (age mean, SOFA median, vasopressor n %), the biggest difference (severity) and their two sentences, and type a class version. Last minute: what the Q2 to Q5 packs add (for example, Q5 has a survivors-only table).

A class version, e.g. 'Of 620 patients, 618 had a day-3 balance and 373 were positive. They were sicker (median SOFA 8 vs 6, vasopressor 55% vs 25%).'

These sentences are the start of a Results section.
:::

Modelled on the running example (a restrictive fluids trial).
:::

- Exposure: restrictive vs usual
- Confounders: age, SOFA, lactate
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Mini-CRF]{.neu-card-title}

- 6 to 10 items
- Units and time points
- 'Unknown' options
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Data dictionary]{.neu-card-title}

- 3 to 5 rows
- Name, label, type, unit or codes
- Allowed values
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Data management]{.neu-card-title}

- Electronic capture (EDC) or double entry
- Coded IDs and an audit trail
- Backups and a data-sharing statement
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Today: what you will collect and how you will keep it safe.
:::

::: {.notes}
Show for 1 minute before modelling, so participants see the expected level.

Variables table first: it drives the CRF, the dictionary and the analysis.

Each participant writes this for their own proposal, not for FLUID-ICU.
:::

::: {.notes}
Proposal builder 5, 30 minutes (21:55-22:25). Template: Research\_Proposal\_Template.docx. Worksheet: Exercise 8.

18 minutes: model live on the running example: variables table, mini-CRF, dictionary rows, data-management plan. 10 minutes: everyone drafts their own variables table alone. Last 2 minutes: call on two or three people to read their outcome and one confounder, and take questions.

Watch for: too many CRF items, outcomes listed as confounders, names in the data file.

::: {.neu-intro}
Three messages to take home.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Design the data]{.neu-card-title}

- Clear CRF items
- Data dictionary first
- Checks at entry
:::

- Log every correction

:::

- Shape decides the summary
- Show every patient
- Table 1 that stands alone

## Extra: Coding, versions, backups and data sharing

::: {.neu-intro}
Four habits that protect your data and your future paper.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Coding]{.neu-card-title}

- Codes, not free text
- Study ID, not names
- Codes in the dictionary
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Versions]{.neu-card-title}

- Raw file: read-only
- Dated copies, e.g. data\_2026-03-12\_v2
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Backups]{.neu-card-title}

- 3 copies on 2 media
- 1 copy off-site, encrypted
- Test a restore
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Data sharing]{.neu-card-title}

- Journals ask for a data-sharing statement
- Plan it at the start
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Never edit the raw file: keep it, copy it, date it, back it up.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Four cheap habits: codes not free text, a read-only raw file with dated copies, 3-2-1 backups, a data-sharing statement planned in the consent form.

Ask: if your laptop were stolen tonight, would your study survive?
:::
